subject: english-literature
title: Love, Identity, Conflict
welcome_lead: Three of the biggest themes in all of literature.
meta_desc: KS3 English Literature adventure on love, identity and conflict themes.
final_note: You can now spot love, identity and conflict in any text.

walkthroughs.body_html: Love shows up as romance, family, friendship or sacrifice. Identify which kind a text explores.
The theme of identity asks who a character really is — under names, masks and others' expectations.
Conflict can be inside (self-doubt) or outside (rival, war, society). It often interlocks with power and identity.

mcqs.q: Who a character truly is = the theme.

options: It means authors can never make mistakes when writing.
The claim that judging a text by what the author 'intended' is fallacious — the text's meaning lies in the work itself, not the author's stated or guessed intentions.
It means it is wrong to write fiction.
A sonnet must always be exactly ten lines long.

mcqs.q: Why are genre conventions important when interpreting a text?
options: It means it is wrong to write fiction.
They set reader expectations the text can fulfil or subvert; analysing how a text uses or breaks conventions reveals its meaning and significance.
Genre is just a label to help bookshops categorise novels.
Genre means whether a book is fiction or non-fiction.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of a Shakespearean sonnet?
options: It means it is wrong to write fiction.
A sonnet is any short love poem.
Fourteen lines in iambic pentameter, structured as three quatrains and a final couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, often with a volta near the couplet.
A sonnet must always be exactly ten lines long.
